title: Cuba vence Canadá e garante vaga olímpica no vôlei
content:
Jogos Olímpicos de Los Angeles 2028: seleção masculina de vôlei de Cuba garantiu neste domingo, 20, uma vaga no campeonato (SOPA Images/Getty Images)
Repórter de Casual
Publicado em 20 de setembro de 2026 às 15h45.
A seleção masculina de vôlei de Cuba garantiu neste domingo, 20, uma vaga nos Jogos Olímpicos de Los Angeles 2028 ao derrotar o Canadá na final do torneio classificatório disputado em Moncton, no país norte-americano, segundo a EFE.
A equipe cubana venceu os canadenses por 3 sets a 1, com parciais de 25-21, 25-23, 23-25 e 25-22, e conquistou o único lugar em disputa para a próxima edição olímpica no Campeonato Continental da Norceca (América do Norte, Central e Caribe).
A imprensa estatal cubana destacou o retorno da seleção masculina de vôlei aos Jogos Olímpicos, com manchetes como "Vôlei masculino cubano retorna aos Jogos Olímpicos" e "Cuba garante classificação olímpica de seu vôlei".
O jornal cubano Granma classificou a vitória como uma revanche esportiva, após a equipe ter ficado fora das edições de Tóquio 2020 e Paris 2024. A publicação afirmou que o grupo transformou a terceira tentativa de classificação em um retorno ao palco olímpico, após a última participação em Rio 2016.
O presidente de Cuba, Miguel Díaz-Canel, também parabenizou a equipe pelas redes sociais. "Volta o vôlei cubano aos Jogos Olímpicos. Em quadra canadense, diante do mesmo rival que um dia tirou nosso sonho, desta vez não houve lamento", escreveu.
A vitória também teve destaque por superar uma derrota recente para o Canadá. Segundo o site Cubadebate, os canadenses haviam vencido Cuba por 3 sets a 0 nas semifinais do Campeonato Continental Norceca realizado no mesmo local.
Na conquista da vaga, os veículos cubanos destacaram as atuações de Yant e López, apontados como líderes da equipe, além dos 14 pontos de Alejandro Miguel González, da defesa de Yonder García e dos nove pontos de Robertlandy Simón, considerado um dos principais centrais da história do vôlei.

title: The human hands that keep this iconic clock ticking
content:
More than a timepiece, it has become a familiar witness to the city’s history, its chimes accompanying generations of Malaysians through moments both ordinary and momentous.
Today, the task of keeping it running falls to three men who continue the work of custodians before them.
Muhammad Kamarul Azman, L Kumarasamy and Roshdihisham Hassan, from the survey and mapping department, check, clean, wind and lubricate the century-old mechanism throughout the year.
“Every evening after office hours, we come here to wind the clock and make sure the time is accurate,” Kamarul told FMT.
Inside the narrow, sweltering tower, the trio take turns working the giant weights that keep the Gillett & Johnston clock ticking.
The task requires patience. According to Kamarul, the crank cannot be turned too quickly, as doing so could disrupt the pulley system. “That is why we rely on our own physical strength,” he said.
Their responsibility does not always end when the day’s checks are done. On one occasion, Kamarul had already returned home when a call came through informing him that the clock had stopped.
“I had already reached home when the building management called. So we had to come back at midnight to inspect it,” he recalled.
Their work takes on added meaning on the eve of Merdeka celebrations, when the clock becomes part of a national moment.
As crowds gather outside and the countdown begins, Kamarul, Kumarasamy and Roshdihisham stay inside the tower, watching closely to make sure the clock reaches midnight precisely as it should.
“At midnight, we really feel nervous. When we hear the people outside counting down, we feel proud from inside the tower,” Kamarul said.
It is a moment that turns an otherwise unseen job into something deeply personal: while thousands celebrate below, the men inside know the clock’s familiar chime depends, in part, on their hands.
Learning from those before them
For Kamarul, the role began almost by chance. When a senior colleague introduced him to the clock, seeing its century-old machinery at work sparked a fascination he had not expected.
“When you watch all the gears and machinery moving, you become very interested in learning how it all works. That is what has kept us here until today.”
There was no handbook to guide them; instead, much of what they know was learnt through experience and from those who cared for the clock before them.
And this knowledge matters because keeping the mechanism alive is not as simple as replacing a broken part.
“If any component is damaged, a replacement has to be specially made according to the original specifications because the parts are no longer available on the market,” Kamarul noted.
And so, year after year, the clock in this iconic building continues to tick – not only because of the machinery inside it, but because of the people who keep watch over it.

title: President seeks deeper relations with Eswatini
content:
President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday called for deeper cooperation between Taiwan and Eswatini and thanked the African kingdom’s deputy prime minister for helping ensure his visit in May went smoothly.
At a meeting with Eswatini Deputy Prime Minister Thulisile Dladla at the Presidential Office in Taipei, Lai said he hoped the two countries would deepen cooperation in disaster management, industry, public health and talent development.
Eswatini is one of Taiwan’s 12 diplomatic allies and its only ally in Africa. The two countries have maintained diplomatic ties for 58 years.
Photo: Screen grab from the Presidential Office’s Flickr page
Dladla is visiting Taiwan after attending Saturday’s inauguration of the World Alliance for Disaster Management (WADM), an initiative launched by Taiwan and of which Eswatini is a founding member.
“Under the framework of the WADM, Taiwan will share disaster prevention technologies, disaster response and rescue experience with Eswatini and other like-minded countries,” Lai said.
Lai also used the meeting to recall his May visit to Eswatini, which had originally been scheduled for April.
The trip was postponed after Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar withdrew permission for Lai’s chartered aircraft to fly through their airspace.
The Presidential Office attributed the withdrawal of the flight permits to pressure from China.
Lai thanked King Mswati III, the Queen Mother and Dladla for helping make the rescheduled trip possible.
“Deputy Prime Minister Dladla personally accompanied our delegation, traveling tens of thousands of kilometers with us to ensure that our journey there and back proceeded smoothly,” Lai said.
Dladla accompanied Lai’s delegation on the May 2-5 trip, during which they traveled about 25,000km aboard King Mswati III’s aircraft before returning to Taiwan.
Dladla called on Taiwan and Eswatini to expand the “scale, speed and breadth” of their cooperation.
The two sides should focus more on investment, industrial development and energy security, as well as mutually beneficial economic opportunities such as mining, she said.
Dladla also thanked Taiwan for increasing rice assistance to Eswatini as the country prepares for possible severe El Nino conditions.
El Nino can cause drought in southern Africa, threatening crop production. Dladla also expressed appreciation for Taiwan’s support for additional social housing for vulnerable communities.
On the WADM, Dladla said Eswatini intended to help make the alliance “a practical platform for capacity building, knowledge sharing and coordinated action.”

title: NIA assures sufficient water supply as strong El Niño draws near
content:
NIA assures sufficient water supply as strong El Niño draws near
The National Irrigation Authority (NIA) said on Sunday that adequate irrigation water is available as a strong El Niño approaches, adding that it will maintain a double dry cropping calendar to maximize the dry season.
In an interview with Super Radyo dzBB, NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen said the agency actually prefers sunny weather, which is why it is implementing double dry cropping.
“Sa pagsasaka po, sa pagtatanim natin, mas gusto nga po ng NIA ‘yung maaraw, kaya nga po binabago ng NIA ‘yung ating cropping calendar, ginagawa po naming… double dry cropping,” Guillen said.
(When it comes to farming, NIA actually prefers sunny weather. That is why NIA is shifting our cropping calendar and implementing… double dry cropping.)
“... Ang ginagawa po ng NIA ngayon, dinadala natin ‘yung ating cropping sa parteng October, aani tayo ng January, tanim ulit tayo ng March [at] aani ulit tayo ng June. So ‘yan po ‘yung tinatawag [na] double dry cropping,” he added.
(What NIA is doing now is shifting our cropping schedule to around October so we can harvest in January, then plant again in March and harvest in June. So that is what we call double dry cropping.)
Guillen pointed out that this system differs from the previous wet and dry cropping calendar, where planting started in November or December, harvest took place in March, and replanting occurred in July.
He explained that sunny weather yields higher crop output through photosynthesis, which relies on sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. However, he emphasized that a sufficient water supply remains crucial to sustain crop growth.
Citing PAGASA, Guillen said the effects of the strong El Niño are projected to be felt in the last quarter of the year, between October and December, and will persist until the second quarter of 2027.
NIA stated that storing water is one of the key ways the agency prepares, making high dams like Magat Dam in Isabela vital to operations.
Guillen said the Magat Dam is almost full and is expected to supply irrigation to 90,000 hectares of farmland.
Meanwhile, Pantabangan Dam in Nueva Ecija, which supplies water to five areas in Luzon, is also nearly full and capable of irrigating around 120,000 hectares.
High-value crops
As part of its preparations, NIA highlighted the importance of coordination with the Department of Agriculture (DA) to jointly identify areas likely to face water shortages.
“Doon sa mga irrigated areas natin alam po ng NIA kung ilan ‘yung kaya niyang patubigan, na tataniman po natin ng palay. Kasi yung palay matakaw po sa tubig ‘yan,” Guillen said.
(In our irrigated areas, NIA knows how many hectares can be supplied with water for rice production, which requires a substantial amount of water.)
“Now, kaya po sinusulong… ‘yung masusing koordinasyon namin ng Department of Agriculture, dahil po pag na-identify namin ‘yung mga areas na kukulangin po ng patubig, marami naman po tayong pwedeng itanim na high-value crops diyan,” he added.
(That is why we are pushing for close coordination with the Department of Agriculture. Once we identify areas that will lack irrigation, we can plant various high-value crops there instead.)
Among the high-value crops he mentioned were corn and mung beans (munggo).
Guillen clarified that a lack of full irrigation does not mean fields must remain unplanted, emphasizing the critical role of interagency coordination.
NIA also urged collaboration with other government agencies, including the Department of Labor and Employment and the Department of Social Welfare and Development, to provide additional intervention measures once El Niño hits.
Farming along irrigation canals
NIA assured the public that irrigation shortages will not cause food prices to increase.
The agency highlighted its program promoting vegetable planting along irrigation canals.
“Pagkahaba-haba po ng ilang, daang libong kilometro po ang ating irrigation sa buong Pilipinas, eh kung magsipag lang yung ating mga farmers, yung ating mga irrigators association at magtanim po sa mga gilid ng irrigation natin ay malaking bagay po yan,” Guillen said.
(We have hundreds of thousands of kilometers of irrigation canals across the Philippines. If our farmers and irrigators' associations actively plant along the banks of these canals, it will be a huge help.)
Guillen said that from 2023 to 2025, vegetable farming along irrigation canals generated P1.6 billion in extra income for farmers nationwide. —RF, GMA News

title: Early voting begins in U.S. midterm elections in race that will shape control of Congress
content:
In-person voting for this year’s midterm elections began Friday, ushering in the final six weeks for Americans to decide which party they trust to lead Congress through a cost-of-living crisis, a prolonged war in Iran and other pressing issues.
Election administrators say they are prepared and confident the vote will be accurate and secure. Nevertheless, President Donald Trump has continued efforts to denigrate certain voting methods and reshape how elections are run, through court challenges, a federal hunt for noncitizen voters and a pressure campaign to force election officials to share sensitive voter data.
Friday marked the start of early voting in Virginia. Voters in a few other states, including Minnesota and South Dakota, can cast absentee ballots in person, typically at a local election office or voting centre. More expansive early voting is scheduled to begin in those and other states in the coming weeks.
At a voting location in Fairfax, Virginia, 18-year-old college student Sanya Singhal was among the first to vote early in person Friday morning, arriving well before the site opened to get in line.
“Why not just have a little fun in life, you know, try to be the first early voter?” she said. “I really want to participate in my democracy.”
Six weeks before the U.S. midterms in November, AI has become a hot political issue
At a voting location in suburban Richmond, a poll worker rang a bell as the building opened and about a dozen voters in line began to file in. Stephen Gura was excited to be the first.
“This election is critical. We need to stop the Trump agenda,” said Gura, who added that he voted for U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, a Democrat, and Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee against Republican incumbent Rob Wittman in the 1st Congressional District.
The Nov. 3 election includes votes for governor and state legislature in most states and will determine whether Republicans maintain control of the U.S. House and Senate. If Democrats retake Congress, it will alter the trajectory of the final two years of Trump’s term, most likely leading to investigations and other oversight efforts.
Voting under way after Trump’s bid to control how elections are run
At the suburban Richmond voting centre, a steady stream of voters flowed in and out. William Curry, a 74-year-old retiree who described himself as a libertarian-leaning independent conservative, voted for Warner’s Republican challenger, Bert Mizusawa, and Wittman. Curry said he generally approves of the job Trump has done, apart from the war with Iran.
“He’s in a mess he can’t get rid of,” Curry said of the conflict.
On a rainy day in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Bill Goehring, 67, said he voted early at the county office because he will be travelling later. He voted for a mix of Democrats and independents, and said Trump’s “dictatorial tendencies are bad for America.”
John Thomas, a conservative retired police officer at the Sioux Falls office, said his biggest concerns were public safety and election integrity. He said he doesn’t want to see immigrants in the country illegally voting in federal elections.
Democrats, activists plan to resist if Trump tries to interfere in midterm elections
The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst and division among many Americans about issues including rising gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, the looming risks of artificial intelligence and Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement campaign.
It also follows an unprecedented spate of mid-decade redistricting for the U.S. House that began when Trump urged the Republican-controlled legislature in Texas to redraw its congressional map to help the party. California and other states followed.
The changes affect millions of people: Research shows 1 in 10 Americans this fall is a resident of a different congressional district than in 2024.
Those partisan efforts are expected to continue before the 2028 elections after a landmark ruling this year from the U.S. Supreme Court weakened the federal Voting Rights Act’s protections against racially discriminatory redistricting.
As the start of early voting approached, Trump was focused on efforts to assert federal control over election administration, even as the Constitution bestows the power to run elections on the states and, in some cases, Congress. The nation’s highest court this week rejected Trump’s bid to restrict mail ballots, but several of his administration’s other efforts to influence the voting process and investigate state voter lists continue.
Virginia’s attorney-general said Thursday that Trump’s administration may have violated the state’s laws after a whistleblower accused federal employees of misrepresenting themselves on voter lookup tools to hunt for noncitizen voters. In a letter, Attorney-General Jay Jones demanded that the Department of Homeland Security confirm whether it had directed anyone to access Virginia voters’ information without first obtaining permission from those voters.
Trump for years has raised the spectre of widespread noncitizen voting in U.S. elections, and this year is no exception. But research continues to show noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.
David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said he wouldn’t be surprised if the Republican president continues “his disinformation campaign and his attack on election officials.” But he said he thinks “the process will hold as it has in past years.”
At least a few Friday voters were motivated to vote early in part because of Trump’s actions.
Opinion: As the midterms loom, Donald Trump tries the art of the steal
In Minneapolis, 47-year-old business processing engineer Dragan Colakovic said he didn’t want to wait until Election Day for fear of being stopped by immigration agents. He said Trump’s surge of agents to Minnesota in an immigration crackdown earlier this year terrified him, a naturalized U.S. citizen who moved from Bosnia in 1997 and saw the horrors of war in the former Yugoslavia.
Sixty-three-year-old Democratic voter Laura Bland in Virginia’s Henrico County said she cast a ballot early to send “a signal that we’re still here” amid Trump’s efforts to curtail mail voting.
“Regardless of whether you vote for a Democrat, Republican, people are not going to be stopped or intimidated from participating in our elections,” Bland said, nearly moved to tears.
Advocates suggest voters cast their ballots early
Voting rights advocates have encouraged voters this year to cast mail ballots early, in part because of concerns about recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations that could delay the application of postmarks to ballots.
Voting early “gives voters options, eases lines on Election Day and can even mean faster results,” said Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of the voting rights group All Voting Is Local.
The top official at the U.S. Postal Service also encouraged voters who cast ballots by mail to get them in a week before they’re due.
“Everything is solved if people vote early,” postmaster general David Steiner said in an interview.
In a news briefing Thursday, Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon urged people not to be swayed by stories they might have seen or read that cast doubt on election operations. They would be able to vote “just like they always have,” he said.
“I just want to reaffirm that Minnesota’s elections are fundamentally free, fair, accurate, honest and secure,” he said.

title: Raccolta dati sulla posizione: multa di 403 milioni a Google
content:
La Data Protection Commission (DPC) dell’Irlanda ha inflitto una sanzione di 403 milioni di euro a Google per la raccolta illegale dei dati sulla posizione attraverso tre funzionalità dell’account. Si tratta del risultato dell’indagine avviata dall’autorità oltre sei anni fa, dopo aver ricevuto una denuncia da 8 organizzazioni che difendono i diritti dei consumatori. L’azienda di Mountain View ha dichiarato che i tool sono stati aggiornati per consentire un maggiore controllo agli utenti.
Violazione della privacy con la raccolta e la conservazione dei dati
La denuncia era stata presentata a fine novembre 2018 dalle associazioni dei consumatori di Norvegia, Olanda, Grecia, Repubblica Ceca, Slovenia, Polonia, Svezia e Danimarca, iscritte alla European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), sulla base di una ricerca pubblicata dai norvegesi del Forbrukerrådet (Norwegian Consumer Council) che evidenziava le pratiche ingannevoli di Google.
La DPC dell’Irlanda ha quindi avviato l’indagine a febbraio 2020 per esaminare le modalità di raccolta dei dati sulla posizione attraverso tre funzionalità dell’account Google: Web & App Activity (Attività web e app), Location History (Cronologia della posizione) e Location Accuracy (Precisione della posizione).
Utilizzando il tracciamento della posizione, Google avrebbe ottenuto informazioni sensibili, come convinzioni religiose, orientamento politico, condizioni di salute e orientamento sessuale. Questi dati sarebbero stati sfruttati per creare un profilo dell’utente e mostrare inserzioni personalizzate. L’azienda californiana avrebbe usato un design ingannevole e fornito informazioni poco chiare sulle tre funzionalità.
Al termine dell’indagine, la DPC ha accertato la violazione del GDPR (Regolamento generale sulla protezione dei dati) con quattro attività:
- Trattamento illecito dei dati di geolocalizzazione con le funzionalità Web & App Activity e Location History
- Mancanza di liceità, correttezza e trasparenza in relazione al trattamento dei dati personali con la funzionalità Location Accuracy
- Mancato rispetto degli obblighi di trasparenza relativi alle tre funzionalità suindicate
- Conservazione dei dati di geolocalizzazione con le funzionalità Web & App Activity e Location History
L’autorità irlandese ha pertanto inflitto a Google una sanzione di 403 milioni di euro e ordinato di apportare modifiche per rispettare la legge entro sei mesi.
Un portavoce dell’azienda di Mountain View ha dichiarato che il caso riguarda vecchie impostazioni che sono state già aggiornate. Dal 2019 sono disponibili tool migliori che semplificano la gestione dei dati di localizzazione. BEUC ha ovviamente festeggiato la decisione, ricordando però che è arrivata dopo quasi 8 anni e che nel 2022 è stata presentata un’altra denuncia per l’uso di un design ingannevole.

title: People with dementia want to participate in research, according to study
content:
For a long time, dementia research has been shaped by concerns that participation may be too burdensome for people with cognitive impairment. However, a recent study led by professors Eino Solje and Anna Mäki-Petäjä-Leinonen found the opposite: 90% of participants reported no burden from participating. Many described the experience as positive, interesting and even refreshing.
The study, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, examined the feasibility and acceptability of a novel research approach known as the Law Clinic Study. The model brings together medical, neuropsychological and legal perspectives in dementia research. Its aim is to improve understanding of how dementia affects an individual's legal status, legal capacity, decision-making abilities and the realization of their rights.
"The pilot study included 20 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or another progressive neurocognitive disorder, together with their spouses. During a single study visit, participants completed an extensive legal interview as well as neuropsychological assessments. At the end of the study day, they were asked to evaluate their experiences of participation," explains postdoctoral researcher Kaisa Näkki, who conducted the research interviews.
"It is essential that issues related to dementia, including legal capacity, are examined through genuinely multidisciplinary research. To the best of our knowledge, research of this kind has not previously been conducted either in Finland or internationally. The findings are highly encouraging and demonstrate that multidisciplinary research can generate knowledge that is also valuable in health care, service systems and societal decision-making," says Solje.
The results showed that participants particularly valued the opportunity for people with dementia to be heard in research concerning their own lives. Many felt that participation enabled them to contribute to improving the situation of people who develop dementia in the future and their families, while also increasing societal understanding of dementia.
The study also found that interviewing people with dementia and their caregivers separately was a crucial element of the research design. Separate interviews facilitated open discussion and ensured that both parties' perspectives could be heard. Caregivers, in particular, felt that being interviewed separately made it easier to discuss sensitive issues.
"The findings challenge persistent stereotypes suggesting that people with dementia are unable to participate in research or evaluate their own experiences. On the contrary, our study demonstrates that carefully designed research that takes participants' needs into account can provide people with dementia with opportunities to be heard and to contribute to knowledge that is relevant to society," says postdoctoral researcher Henna Nikumaa, who analyzed the interview data.
The Law Clinic Study represents an internationally distinctive initiative, combining legal and medical research in the field of dementia. According to the researchers, this multidisciplinary approach is capable of generating new insights into questions that might be difficult to address from the perspective of a single discipline.
"Following this successful pilot phase, our goal is to expand the study to a larger patient population. In particular, we aim to develop methods for assessing the legal capacity of people with dementia, as no established practices or uniform assessment criteria currently exist," says Mäki-Petäjä-Leinonen.

title: Agentic Governance and Adversarial Verification for Policy-Constrained LLM Healthcare Appeal Generation
content: Claim denial management costs U.S. healthcare approximately $260 billion annually in administrative overhead. Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can produce fluent clinical text, but single-agent architectures fail in high-stakes healthcare: they introduce unsupported clinical details and lose the logical structure of hierarchical payer policy. We propose AGVF (Agentic Governance and Adversarial Verification Framework), a multi-agent architecture for medical-necessity appeal generation under explicit policy and evidence constraints. AGVF models appeal synthesis as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) over five agents: policy formalization, evidence retrieval, gap analysis, adversarial critique, and gated synthesis. We prove that refinement over a fixed policy constraint graph monotonically reduces evidence-deficiency and terminates with either a complete satisfying frontier or a localized evidence gap. A deterministic citation- grounding gate prevents assertions without admissible evidence from entering shared state. We provide a reference implementation and validate it on 1,000 synthetic appeal cases parameterized from de-identified public hospital discharge data. The validation confirms zero citation-grounding violations across all AGVF cases and monotone deficiency reduction in every episode; ablating the gate raises violations to 100%, confirming it is load-bearing. The study uses no real patient records and does not measure clinical efficacy. AGVF thus contributes a theory-backed agentic architecture and verified reference implementation for policy-constrained LLM generation in healthcare.

title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship

American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally.
Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide.
Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax
— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026
“I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.”
Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”.
“I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.”
Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”.
Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania.
During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter.
In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family.
American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today”
He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026
There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it.
The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed.
Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland.
Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik.
Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US.
The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026
The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live.
The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship.
One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics.
Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.
Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026
Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342.
However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty.
Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland.
Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage.

title: Perhaps Malaysians are a lot kinder than we think
content:
A middle-aged Chinese woman from an NGO walked into the newsroom, seeking help.
A journalist of Indian descent was assigned to write the story — that of a young Malay girl who urgently needed medical attention.
This story, recounted by FMT executive chairman Nelson Fernandez at a forum recently, would have just been another account of how Malaysians help each other.
But this was different. People of all races came together to answer a call for help by a Chinese, disseminated by an Indian to help a Malay.
Within hours of FMT publishing the story, up to RM150,000 had been pledged, taking little Diya Amanda on her first step towards a normal childhood.
But for Fernandez, it was just another day at the office.
The Malaysia we keep saying we want is already here.
Nobody ever needed a campaign or matching T-shirts to foster unity. Nobody asked who prayed where or what box they ticked on a form.
This was simply a child who needed help.
And people came forward.
Back in 1982, Paul McCartney and Stevie Wonder sang a lovely song about “Ebony and Ivory” living together in perfect harmony. If black and white piano keys could exist in harmony, surely human beings could figure it out too.
More than forty years later, humanity is still working on it.
We, Malaysians, have spent decades talking about unity. We have slogans, campaigns and speeches about it. We have probably printed enough banners about togetherness to wrap around the country several times over.
Yet one of the best demonstrations of Malaysian unity happened without anybody needing to announce it.
Just like the song, maybe harmony doesn’t require every key to sound the same.
I don’t think Malaysia suffers from an absence of harmony. Perhaps we suffer from not seeing enough of it.
That matters because the stories we repeatedly hear about one another influence the nation we are a part of.
If Malaysians constantly encounter one another through anger, suspicion and confrontation, eventually it becomes easy to believe we are fundamentally divided.
This is why Fernandez’s argument about journalism matters beyond journalism.
He wasn’t suggesting difficult stories shouldn’t be told. Nor should they be.
He was asking for something harder: that conflict does not become the only lens through which Malaysians see one another.
We should be able to disagree fiercely without dehumanising others. We should be able to defend what we believe without humiliating someone who believes differently.
And when we report what divides Malaysia, we should not forget the stories that reveal what still holds us together.
That responsibility isn’t just journalists’ anymore.
Every one of us carries a tiny newsroom in our pockets. We decide what gets shared, forwarded and viral-ed.
Fernandez said something else at the New Muslim Community Conference in Kuala Lumpur, that stayed with me:
“Everyone talks about religion, but no one talks about love, compassion and kindness.”
Love. Compassion. Kindness.
Three words that might seem soft beside politics, race, religion and power.
But as I wrote in my previous article, we have grossly misunderstood softness and strength.
It is easy to be kind to people who agree with us and who are similar and familiar. It takes something stronger to extend that kindness to someone who isn’t.
Perhaps Malaysians do not need to agree on everything and maybe agreement was never the point.
Harmony isn’t everyone singing the same note. That’s unison.
Harmony requires difference.
Ebony and ivory don’t create music because they overcame their differences. Their differences are the point.
Malaysia isn’t so different. A unique colourful country like ours was never going to be one note.
I believe we should stop trying to make everyone sound the same and become better at hearing one another instead.
That’s where harmony begins.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

title: 'I'm forever grateful for my girl's donated heart'
content:
'I'm forever grateful for my girl's donated heart'
- Published
Ahead of Organ Donation Week, two mothers whose children were involved in transplants share their stories from either side of the experience.
Seven-year-old Evie is thriving.
She is doing well at school, enjoys playing with friends and is keen to give everything a go, her mother Chloe Green says.
But for her daughter to be doing so well today, another family had to go through the unimaginable pain of losing their child.
When she was three years old, Evie needed a new heart.
The toddler from Middlesbrough spent 16 months in hospital in Newcastle being kept alive by a Berlin Heart, a mechanical pump which she had to be permanently attached to.
Evie featured in a project by Consett-based photographer Debbie Todd, taking before and after pictures of children awaiting life-saving organs.
Sadly, Debbie says, not all the children got their "after" picture.
Evie's wait was so long she ended up having three "before" photos taken, images treasured by Chloe as showing the journey her daughter had to undertake.
Chloe, 31, and her husband David, 38, would swap places by her hospital bedside, juggling looking after her with work and caring for their other child, Evie's brother Theo, who is a year older than his sister.
Chloe says she tried to stay optimistic, focusing on "small wins all the time", but her mindset changed when Evie had to be attached to the machine.
"I was watching her dying," Chloe says. "Suddenly my priority was 'we need a new heart'."
She understood what that meant for any potential donor.
"I did feel I was in a moral quandary," Chloe says. "It comes with a lot of guilt.
"Of course you are not wanting someone else to die, but the doctors said we could only think of what we needed for Evie's treatment plan, you have to have that boundary."
They were waiting for another family to do an "amazing thing", Chloe says, and the appreciation never fades.
"Whenever I reflect back or see Evie hitting a milestone, I think of that [donor] child," she says.
"I almost feel like they are part of our family, they are coming along with us."
The donated heart was a "perfect match" for Evie and has "done so much for her", Chloe says.
She acknowledges that may not fully comfort the donor's family but might give them some peace to know.
Chloe does not know who the donor was but has written a letter to their family, there for them to read should they ever choose to.
"If I could speak to the donor's family, I would just be forever thanking them," Chloe says.
"We would love to share everything about Evie's life if they were willing to, but of course it has to be their choice.
"It would just be constant gratitude. I am forever grateful to them."
Anna-Louise Bates knows what it is like to receive such a letter.
In 2015, her husband Stuart and seven-year-old son Fraser were killed when they were hit by a car near their home in Talbot Green in south Wales.
Because he died at the scene, Stuart, who had signed the organ registry and wanted to be a donor, was unable to be one.
But Fraser's heart, lungs, liver and kidneys were given to three other children and an adult, with his heart going to a young twin boy from Hartlepool called Roman.
"I won't forget the first letter I ever received from his mum," Anna-Louise says. "How the loss of my boy had allowed hers to grow.
"To know Fraser lives on has given me so much hope, it was like they didn't die in vain.
"Life is a gift and the biggest gift you can give is life."
She said milestones such as Fraser's recent 18th birthday were "incredibly difficult", but hearing of Roman enjoying life and having "10 years' worth of memories and love" gave "some comfort".
Anna-Louise founded Believe Organ Donor Support, to encourage people to think about organ donation and discuss it with their loved ones.
At Stuart's insistence, she and her husband had the "icky" conversation just two weeks before the crash, and Anna-Louise is so grateful they did.
It meant in that "24 hours of hell", the questions around organ donation were the "only time I didn't have to think", she says.
Knowing her husband's wishes and how her son was meant she felt confident to agree to donate, with the lives Fraser saved "a testament to the big heart he had".
She has in the years since thought about it from the recipient's point of view, she says, about how a parent might feel knowing a "young child passed away for you to have that organ".
"The way I reconcile that is I am just pleased Fraser's gift has allowed a child to live on," she says.
"He gave the greatest gift and especially because this was so close to Christmas, he gave the gift of life that he could no longer be part of."
She says she is not telling everyone they have to be a donor, but is encouraging people to "have those conversations" and register their preference on the organ donation registry so their loved ones know their wishes.
Anna-Louise has spoken to many children since and found they were "really open" to organ donation and more willing to discuss it than their adult parents, she says.
According to the NHS, some 408 people died last year while on the UK transplant waiting list, with Anna-Louise saying just 1% of people end up being eligible to be a donor.
Since 2015 in Wales, 2020 in England and 2021 in Scotland, authorities have operated an opt-out service, external, where adults are presumed to be donors unless they declare otherwise on the NHS Organ Donation Register.
But families will still be consulted and can object.
The system does not apply to people under 18 and decisions regarding children are made by their families, although anyone of any age can add themselves to the register.
Chloe in Middlesbrough is also asking people to think about it in advance, what would they do if the unthinkable happened?
"You do not want to think about your child dying, I understand that" she says.
"But look at the children doing well, what can come from thinking about it and making that decision to donate.
"I totally respect people's choices.
"It's just about thinking and talking about it."

title: Autonomisation des femmes de Dahra : le ministre Idrissa Samb remet des attestations de formation et des bons de financements à 306 femmes
content:
Autonomisation des femmes de Dahra : le ministre Idrissa Samb remet des attestations de formation et des bons de financements à 306 femmes
Le projet de formation professionnelle et d’insertion ( PFPI) mis en œuvre par Education Developement Center Senegal ( EDC Senegal ) avec l’appui technique et financier de la fondation Mastercard en partenariat avec la direction générale de la formation professionnelle et technique (DGFPT), la direction de l’insertion et la Direction de l’apprentissage du ministère de l’emploi et de la formation professionnelle et Technique a organisé ce vendredi une cérémonie de remise d’attestations de formation et de bons de financements au profit de 306 femmes de la commune de Dahra Djoloff dans le département de Linguère.
Cette cérémonie présidée par le ministre de la formation professionnelle et Technique Idrissa Samb s’inscrit dans le cadre des activités du PFPI, dont la poursuite du financement et de l’accompagnement des jeunes et des femmes à travers un fonds d’amorçage d’un montant de 863 millions de francs pour l’année 2026.
Au-delà de la remise symbolique des attestations et des bons de financement, cette rencontre est un moment de mobilisation de valorisation et d’engagement collectif en faveur de l’insertion socio-professionnelle et de l’autonomisation économique des femmes.
Il faut signaler que ces 306 femmes regroupées autour de neuf groupements qui reçoivent aujourd’hui leurs attestations de formation ont été auparavant initiées aux techniques de fabrication de savon, d’eau de javel, de transformations de fruits et légumes et des produits laitiers. Chaque regroupement féminin a reçu 750.000 FCFA pour un montant
Selon le ministre ces financements permettront à ces bonnes dames de créer, développer ou consolider leurs activités économiques et de renforcer leur autonomisation économique en favorisant leur accès à l’emploi et à l’entrepreneuriat. Il a par ailleurs demandé aux bénéficiaires d’utiliser à bon escient ce fonds.
Les bénéficiaires visiblement très satisfaits ont remercié l’état du Sénégal à travers le ministère de la formation professionnelle et technique pour leur avoir octroyé ces financements en vue de renforcer davantage leurs activités.
